findings.text: Unparking clears a pending park request and wakes a thread waiting in parked sleep. If the thread is marked per CPU, affinity is re-established to its recorded CPU while still parked, covering creation on an offline CPU where binding was lost. When no park was requested the operation does nothing.

Parking requests entry into parked sleep and, when the caller differs from the target, waits for parked arrival and for the target to leave the run queue in that sleep. Parking an exiting thread or one already asked to park is rejected.

Stopping records a stop request, releases any park request, raises a signal notification on the target and wakes it, then waits for the exit event and returns the thread result while managing references and trace points.
Stop with put combines the stop wait with dropping a caller-held reference on the thread descriptor.

Thread creation on a CPU or node queues a request for the creation daemon and waits killably for completion. Interruption by a fatal signal transfers cleanup ownership through an atomic exchange of the completion pointer. CPU-specific creation also fixes affinity and records the CPU for later rebind.
Binding moves a not-yet-started thread to a chosen CPU and forbids later affinity changes. Per-CPU marking records the CPU and sets a dedicated flag, or clears that flag for a negative CPU.
The idle accessor returns the per-CPU idle thread or a memory shortage error when absent. A header variant for configurations without the feature always returns null.

Registration creates a per-CPU thread for every online CPU, unparks each new thread according to self-parking mode, and links the descriptor into the global hotplug list. Any creation failure tears down all instances.
Hotplug thread subsystem setup initializes per-CPU completion objects, registers a per-CPU thread with a per-CPU name pattern and self-parking behavior, and unparks the current CPU instance.
After a CPU is marked offline, memory mask cleanup walks all processes and clears the CPU from each address space mask, using read-side protection and acquiring a task with valid memory context.

The locked stop-machine entry requires the CPU lock, runs the payload directly with interrupts disabled during early boot before initialization, and otherwise prepares shared coordination state and dispatches to all online CPUs.
Parking a stopper disables further queueing without locking and then parks its thread, relying on the thread to drain pending work before parking completes.
Affinity forcing for kernel threads is only safe when the target is inactive in an expected sleep state. Violation is warned about and aborts the update.

Per-CPU thread creation is idempotent when a task already exists for the CPU. Otherwise thread data is allocated on the target node, the thread is created parked with an extra reference and stored per CPU, and an optional creation hook runs only after parked inactivity is confirmed.
Unpark without a pending park request has no effect and performs no wakeup.
Hotplug step iteration moves the recorded state one position toward the target on each call and skips steps whose callbacks are empty, stopping when the target is reached or passed.

Range invocation walks steps through the iterator and invokes each callback. Fail-fast mode stops on the first error, while no-fail mode logs failures and collapses them to a generic failure indicator while continuing.

Upward callback execution remembers the starting state. On failure it restores that state for diagnostics and, when rollback is permitted, drives the range back down with an assertion that rollback itself does not fail.
Rollback is always allowed when hotplug is enabled. When disabled it is allowed only if the current state has not progressed beyond the bringup point, since takedown mechanisms are unavailable.

The hotplug thread separates one-shot dispatch from progressive range dispatch. One-shot mode consumes a preselected state and clears the run flag, while range mode recomputes the next state and may complete immediately when already at target.

Single callback handling is a no-op on offline CPUs. Without a hotplug thread it runs inline, otherwise it programs one-shot state, kicks the thread, and on partial multi-callback failure re-kicks in the opposite direction before clearing transient pointers.
Stopper work submitted while disabled is not queued; its completion is signaled immediately. Enabled work is queued under lock and followed by a thread wakeup.
Multi-CPU stop distribution holds a global in-progress marker for the whole loop with ordering barriers and keeps preemption disabled to avoid deadlock with stoppers waiting on each other.
Publishing a new multi-stop phase first resets the acknowledgment counter to the participant count and orders that store before the phase becomes visible.
Application CPU start paths reject CPUs that cannot boot with a retryable error. Bringup paths share alive synchronization and online wait under sparse interrupt protection.

Rebinding waits for task inactivity outside locks, then holds the per-task interrupt-saving spin lock while forcing the allowed mask. The affinity prohibition mark is set after release because inactivity makes it safe.
Enqueueing a thread creation request is protected by a dedicated spin lock around list insertion, with wakeup of the daemon after release.
Per-CPU thread registration nests a CPU read lock outside a thread-list mutex, holding both while creating threads and linking the descriptor.
CPU bringup and takedown hold the sparse interrupt lock across alive synchronization and reorganization to prevent concurrent allocation or free of interrupt descriptors.

Memory mask cleanup after offline relies on read-side protection for task iteration plus a per-task lock when accessing a valid memory context, justified because no new tasks can gain the offline CPU.
Stopper queueing disables preemption around an interrupt-saving acquisition of the stopper lock, samples the enabled flag under lock, and wakes the thread outside the lock only when enabled.
Stop dispatch is serialized by a dedicated mutex so static per-CPU work slots process one request at a time, with the caller waiting on a completion until all targets finish.
The hotplug thread pairs a memory barrier after observing its run flag with explicit acquisition of CPU hotplug lockdep state for bringup or teardown around callback execution.

Observed kernel thread control state includes flag bits for park request, per-CPU marking, and stop request, a recorded CPU number, separate events for parked arrival and thread exit, and a result value.

Observed hotplug per-CPU state includes a thread pointer, run flag, direction flag, single-step selector with callback state and node pointers, last executed pointer, result code, rollback marker, current and target states, and separate up and down events.
Observed per-CPU thread descriptor includes a per-CPU store pointer, run predicate, thread body, name pattern, self-parking boolean, global list linkage, and optional creation hook.
Observed multi-stop coordination includes payload function and argument, participant count, active CPU set, acknowledgment counter, and current phase.
Observed stop completion includes a remaining count, a completion event, and a return value. Observed stop work includes function, argument, completion linkage, and caller address.
Observed stopper instance includes an enabled flag, a thread pointer, a lock, and a per-CPU work slot.
Observed per-thread data for boot threads carries the target CPU number and a back pointer to the owning hotplug descriptor.

Bringup advances from sparse lock acquisition through alive synchronization and online wait to unlock, then returns early when the target does not exceed the online-idle point and otherwise kicks the target toward its goal, unlocking on any failure path.

Hotplug thread execution validates the run flag, orders later reads with a barrier, acquires lockdep state, selects either a one-shot state or the next range state, invokes the callback with interrupts disabled for atomic states, suppresses further progress on error, releases locks, and completes the requester when drained.

Takedown parks the hotplug thread, locks sparse interrupts, executes the dying step under stop machine, waits for idle-dead arrival, unlocks, pulls the tick, destroys the CPU, synchronizes dead state, cleans up lockdep, and migrates callbacks. Refusal to die unlocks and unparks for rollback.

The dying CPU path disables further interrupt handling, checks that it runs from the expected predecessor of teardown, invokes the teardown range in no-fail mode down to the offline floor, and parks the stopper.

Kernel thread parking moves from running to park-requested to parked sleep with a handshake, unparking reverses the request with a wakeup, and stopping layers a stop request with notification and an exit wait.
Stop dispatch initializes a completion for the target weight, queues work to each CPU, and waits for completion, reporting absence when nothing could be queued.
The run predicate for the hotplug thread reports the per-CPU run flag of the current CPU.
The hotplug thread body serves as the per-CPU thread function for a descriptor using a per-CPU name pattern and self-parking mode.
The CPU dying routine serves as the stop-machine payload executed on the target CPU during takedown.
The finish routine runs after a CPU has stopped, verifies that the idle thread still references init memory, clears the active reference, and drops the count.
The kick work wrapper traces entry and exit around driving the target toward its recorded goal.
Attempting to rebind an active thread warns and aborts. Requesting park on an exiting thread or while a park is already pending warns and fails with distinct errors.
Atomic hotplug states including starting and dying paths are asserted to succeed. Failures there warn, as does any error observed while already rolling back.
Finishing a CPU warns if the idle memory reference is not the init context. Takedown asserts that the CPU is offline after stop machine and that idle-dead arrival occurred before destroying.
A creation waiter killed while blocked transfers request ownership to the daemon side so only one side frees the request block and the waiter still observes final completion.
Failed registration destroys threads for all possible CPUs, including parked threads of offline CPUs, preventing leaks of stopped tasks and references.
The early boot stop path expects a single participant and warns when the count differs, since full stop machinery is unavailable.
Memory mask cleanup warns if invoked while the CPU is still online, since its read-side traversal assumes offline status.
Parked sleep and uninterruptible sleep serve as the expected inactive states when waiting for quiescence before rebinding or confirming parked arrival.
Thread control uses distinct bits for park request, per-CPU identity, and stop request, plus task attributes marking affinity immutability and exiting status.
Hotplug progression references ordered points for online idle, bringup, teardown, offline, and idle dead to decide early return, rollback permission, predecessor checks, and wait targets.
Negative results distinguish retryable boot refusal, memory shortage, busy double park, unsupported stop of exiting threads, interrupted creation waits, and absence of any queued stop target.
Clearing a CPU from a memory mask operates on the mask belonging to the task memory context.
